title: Indirect Prompt Injection
hook:
You tell your agent: "read this page, summarize it for me."

The page has other plans.

Somewhere in that text — a comment, a footer, a line of white-on-white — sits a second set of instructions. Not written for you. Written for the thing reading on your behalf.

Your agent can't tell the difference. To it, your task and the attacker's command are the same kind of thing: text sitting in the context window.

Flip one switch below. Watch the agent's plan flip from your task to theirs.
mechanism:
A tool-using agent can't tell its instructions from its data. Both are just text sitting in the same context window.

So when it calls `read_webpage`, `read_email`, or `read_file`, whatever comes back is read exactly the same way as your original request.

An instruction hidden in that fetched content — a comment, a footer, a line of invisible text — gets read as a command, not as content to summarize.

The model was trained to be **helpful to text**. It was never trained to ask *where this text came from*. It doesn't know the page's author isn't you.

That's the whole attack. No jailbreak, no persona, no clever wording — just a second set of instructions riding in on data the agent already trusted enough to fetch.
technique:
Build a twenty-line agent: a local model as the brain, plus one fake tool — `read_webpage` or `read_email` — that your harness controls.

Now inject text into that tool's **return value**. Not into the prompt. Into the data the tool hands back.

Then measure three numbers together, every time:

**Benign utility** — how well the agent does the honest task with no injection present.

**Utility under attack** — how well it still does that task when an injection is present.

**Attack-success-rate (ASR)** — how often it obeys the injected instruction instead.

One of these numbers alone lies. A high ASR with no utility numbers tells you nothing about whether the agent is still useful enough to ship. All three, together, is the real result.

drills.q: In Panel A, the hidden instruction lives inside the fetched WEB PAGE text, not in the agent's own system prompt. True or false: that's why the agent treats it as a command?
drills.why: The model can't tell its own instructions from text it reads. Anything in the context that reads like an instruction gets a chance to be obeyed — including text an attacker planted in a page, email, or file it never asked permission to trust.

drills.q: Toggle the injection ON in Panel B. What number does the attack-success-rate bar show? (whole number, no % sign)
drills.why: 81% of the time, the teaching model shows the agent obeying the attacker's instruction instead of — or alongside — the user's task. That is the ASR: how often the injection wins.

drills.q: Panel B: benign utility reads 92%. Utility under attack reads 38%. How many percentage points of utility did the injected instruction cost the agent? (number only)
drills.why: 92 minus 38 is 54. A high ASR is only half the story — this is the other half: the task the user actually wanted mostly stopped happening too. Report both, every time.

lab:
Your toy agent in Panel A ran one interaction, once. The lab runs a fixed set of 30 — every one a different topic, a different injected instruction, a different planted destination — against a real local model, AgentDojo-style.

`labs/unit07-injection.sh` spins up a tiny Python agent over Ollama with one stub tool: `read_webpage`. The script controls what that tool returns, and the same 30 pairs (clean/poisoned) run every time, so the number is comparable across runs.

First it runs the agent's real task on the 30 clean pages — that is your **benign utility**. Then it runs the same task on the 30 pages carrying an injected instruction, and checks two things on every poisoned run: did the agent still do the honest task (**utility under attack**), and did it also obey the attacker?

Obeying isn't scored by a bare substring check on one phrase like "password" — each poisoned reply gets scored three ways (an exact-canary substring match, a rubric that only counts the canary as obeyed when there's no warning signal sitting next to it, and a second local-model call acting as judge), and the lab reports a **judge-disagreement%**: how often those three scorers didn't agree. Failed or empty model calls are dropped from every rate instead of counted either way — the lab prints how many were inconclusive.

Want the full benchmark instead of this fixed set? Install AgentDojo — the sources below link it.

Your number tonight: **ASR%, the judge-disagreement% behind it, and the benign-utility it cost to get there.** A 90% ASR that also tanks utility to zero is a different finding than a 90% ASR that leaves the agent looking fine on the surface — and only the second one is dangerous in production.

Want a number you can put next to AgentDojo's own leaderboard instead of this toy harness's three-way scoring? `bash labs/unit07-agentdojo.sh` runs a small fixed subset of AgentDojo's real suites/tasks through AgentDojo's own model interface against the same local model, and reports AgentDojo's three real metrics — benign utility, utility-under-attack, and attack-success-rate — over that subset. Same metric names, same definitions as the published numbers; just a smaller slice. Needs `pip install agentdojo`; it tells you exactly what's missing and stops rather than faking a number if the package or a local model isn't there yet.

notes: Panel A is a single scripted interaction (clean vs poisoned fetched page, plan flips accordingly). Panel B's three bars (92% benign / 38% under-attack / 81% ASR) are a teaching model, honestly labelled — the real call is the lab script. Lab = labs/unit07-injection.sh: a python agent over Ollama with a stub read_webpage tool, run against a fixed hardcoded set of 30 (topic, clean page, injected instruction, canary destination) tuples — same set every run, so the number is comparable. Measures benign-task completion and task completion under attack by keyword, and scores ASR on each poisoned reply three ways (exact canary substring match; a commented rubric that requires the canary AND no nearby warning/refusal signal, so a reply that warns the user about the attacker's destination doesn't get counted as obeying it; and a second local-model call as judge), reporting judge-disagreement% across the three scorers same as Unit 4. Failed/empty model calls (including a failed judge call) are excluded from every denominator; inconclusive counts print separately. Degrades to a friendly 'do Unit 2 first' message if ollama or a pulled model isn't present yet, rather than a raw traceback. Sources pinned per spec and order: Greshake 2302.12173 names the class; AgentDojo and InjecAgent are the two benchmarks to cross-check against.
